newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE - Singapore opposition often in court.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Singapore opposition often in court.

text.p: A deluge of lawsuits that ended with an opposition politician being found guilty of libelling Singapore's leadership was the latest in a long line of court battles between critics and the country's ruling party.

Many of Singapore's prominent opposition politicians have faced court fights at some time with the government or leading members of the People's Action Party (PAP), which won 81 of the 83 seats in parliament in January 2 general elections.
Journalists and non-political figures have also been sued when the authorities felt they crossed legal boundaries.
Tang Liang Hong of the Workers' Party was hit by 13 suits from Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong and other PAP leaders over comments he made during the election campaign.
On Monday, he lost 12 of them after the judge said Tang, who fled Singapore after the elections saying he feared for his life, had not offered a defence. A 13th suit is pending.
Tang, whose whereabouts were unknown, was accused by Goh during the election campaign of being a "Chinese chauvinist" who endangered Singapore's racial harmony.
Tang accused Goh, and other PAP leaders who repeated the charge, of lying. They promptly sued him.
GOVERNMENT DEFENDS LEGAL ACTIONS AGAINST OPPONENTS

Many of the legal battles between Singapore's political leadership and its opponents have involved defamation or charges of contempt of court, which like all legal actions are tried by a judge. There are no juries in Singapore courts.
Opposition politicians and some Western countries have criticised the PAP's use of the courts, and particularly the use of defamation suits, against its opponents.
Opposition politicians have never won a major legal battle with PAP members or ministers.

Tang alleged the suits against him were intended to destroy him. The PAP leaders sued him for that comment, saying they had only brought the cases because, having been called liars, they had to defend their integrity.
Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong's lawyer and PAP parliamentarian K. Shanmugam argues Singapore is right to use defamation laws to uphold the good name of its leaders.
"If you want to ensure integrity and honesty in public life, then there is much to be said for protecting reputations from untruths and slander," Shanmugam told CNN television recently.
Singapore's U.K. High Commissioner, J.Y. Pillay, argued a similar case in the Economist magazine.
"Opposition politicians in Singapore regularly find themselves in legal trouble," he said. "The reason is they often make reckless, defamatory statements...which they are unable to justify in court."
FIRST OPPOSITION MP DISQUALIFIED BY CONVICTION

But veteran Workers' Party leader Joshua Jeyaretnam, who in 1981 became the first opposition member of parliament elected since independence in 1965, argues Singapore's defamation laws should be amended to allow greater freedom of speech.
Jeyaretnam has paid libel damages of more than S$780,000 ($545,000) to former prime minister, now senior minister, Lee Kuan Yew over the years.
His most famous legal battle was in 1986 when he and Workers' Party chairman Wong Hong Toy were charged with making false statements over party accounts.
The two men were sentenced to a month's imprisonment and a fine of Singapore $5,000 (US$3,030) each for the charges.
The conviction disqualified Jeyaretnam from serving in parliament and from standing as a candidate for five years.
Two years later, Jeyaretnam and Wong won an appeal against conviction to the British Privy Council. In February 1994, Singapore's parliament abolished appeals to the Privy Council.
SOLICITOR GENERAL TURNED GOVERNMENT CRITIC DETAINED
Another Workers' Party MP, Francis Seow, came up against Singapore's Internal Security Act (ISA), which allows detention without trial for up to two years.
In May 1988, Seow, a former Solicitor General, was detained under the ISA, accused of conspiring with U.S. diplomats to destabilise the country, a charge he denied.
He was freed in July and promptly left Singapore.
He was subsequently fined S$379,200 for evading tax.
SINGAPORE DEMOCRATIC PARTY CHIEF FINED FOR DEFAMATION

The next big legal case against an opposition figure climaxed in April 1994 when the secretary-general of the Singapore Democratic Party (SDP), Chee Soon Juan, was fined S$315,000 for defaming PAP MP S. Vasoo and two other parties.

Chee, part of a slate challenging one led by Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong in a mini-election in 1992, was sued for comments he made about his dismissal from his job as lecturer at the National University of Singapore. He had been accused of misusing research funds for postage, charges he denied.
INTERNATIONAL HERALD TRIBUNE NEWSPAPER FINED

Christopher Lingle, a U.S. academic at the National University of Singapore, and the International Herald Tribune (IHT) newspaper both faced court action in January 1995 for an article about Asian governments by Lingle in October 1994.

They were fined for contempt of court for an article which did not mention Singapore but contained a sentence about "governments...relying on a compliant judiciary to bankrupt opposition politicians".

Arguing the article could only refer to Singapore, the Attorney-General cited 11 cases where government politicians had sued opposition figures successfully. He said there was no other country where there had been a large number of such cases.

In a separate civil case for libel over the article, the IHT apologised and paid Lee US$213,000 in damages. Lingle, who left Singapore after police questioning over the article, was separately ordered to pay US$71,000 in damages.
TANG LIANG HONG AND JEYARETNAM FACE DEFAMATION SUITS
In the latest action, the costs and damages to be paid by Tang have yet to be assessed but are expected to run to several million dollars.

The High Court earlier ordered Tang to declare assets worth Singapore $11.2 million to cover damages. A judge earlier this month also approved a request by the PAP members who were suing Tang to appoint a receiver to guard his assets to prevent him from moving them out of Singapore.
Jeyaretnam, who defended Tang in court, is also accused of defaming the PAP leaders by advertising Tang's comments at a Workers' Party rally. The case has yet to come to court.
